newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to probe politicians on loans scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to probe politicians on loans scandal.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors plan to question politicians who have been named by the founder of the stricken Hanbo Group as taking his bribes, a prosecution official said on Wednesday.
He said prosecutors had a list of politicians Chung Tae-soo had confessed to paying off, but declined to give details.
"All politicians in the Chung Tae-soo list will be summoned for questioning," the official said. "When and how they will be investigated will be decided later."
In testimony broadcast live from a Seoul jail on Monday, Chung told a parliamentary inquiry his officials gave money to three politicians -- one each from the ruling party and two opposition groups.

Chung said he understood Hanbo officials paid money to Kim Deog-ryong, a member of President Kim Young-sam's inner circle and one of nine people tipped as the ruling New Korea Party's candidate in presidential polls.
Kim Young-sam is barred from seeking a second term.

Chung said money was also delivered to Kim Sang-hyun, a senior lawmaker with the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, and Kim Yong-hwan, secretary-general of the United Liberal Democrats.
After the hearing, all three politicians denied taking money from Chung.
Chung said that he had given money to a group of other politicians but declined to elaborate.

Domestic media reports say Chung has a list of about 20 politicians he is alleged to have bribed to keep loans rolling in to Hanbo's steelmaking flagship, which ultimately collapsed in January after new money dried up.
Chung is on trial on bribery and other charges along with nine others, including three close associates of President Kim, in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.

In the hearing, Chung also said that he had donated money to President Kim's election campaign, but denied making personal payments to Kim. Chung said his campaign contributions were legal because he was a member of the ruling party's finance committee.
Chung said he gave up to one billion won ($1.12 million) to the ruling party, some of it to fund the 1992 presidential election.
Prosecutors alleged that Chung siphoned off millions of dollars from the bank loans and used it to buy influence with politicians and bankers to secure more loans.

Hanbo expanded rapidly under Kim Young-sam's administration. But the collapse of its steelmaking flagship uncovered a tangled web of corruption that rocked the economy and devastated the president's image.
The hearing, part of a 45-day probe by parliament into South Korea's biggest corporate failure, was arranged after the opposition attacked a probe by prosecutors as a whitewash.
